title: The Steel Ring
lines: Once upon a time there was a poor man.
One day this poor man went into the forest for wood.
As he was picking up dry branches, he picked up a little snake with them.
He wanted to kill it, but the little snake spoke up and said:
"Don't kill me, poor man,
for I will make you happy all your life if you spare my life."
"Come now, what are you saying, little snake?" said the poor man.
"I am not such a silly fool as to believe your promise."
"Oh, but do believe me, poor man, and you will not be sorry.
Here, I give you a steel ring. Put it on your finger,
and if you ever have a wish in your life,
just turn this ring around on your finger,
and I will be there at once and grant your wish."
"So be it," thought the poor man. "If it does no good,
it does no harm." He took the ring, put it on his finger, and went home.
He had hardly settled down at home
when he turned the ring on his finger, and there was the little snake.
"What is your command, dear master?"
"My command is this," said the poor man,
"by tomorrow morning, make me a palace here
such as not even the Turkish emperor has."
"It shall be done, dear master," said the little snake,
and it vanished as if the earth had swallowed it.
Well, that evening the poor man went to bed and slept like a log.
When he woke in the morning, his eyes and mouth fell wide open,
for a shining palace had risen in place of his ragged little hut.
It was such as no human eye had ever seen in this world!
Everything around was pure gold, every single thing.
Even the table was gold,
and in its middle stood a dish of pure gold as big as a cart wheel.
"Well," said the poor man to himself, "that little snake did not trick me after all.
My, how wise I was to spare its life!"
Again he turned the ring, and that very moment the little snake was there.
"What is your command, dear master?"
"My command is that you bring me the Black King's daughter to be my wife."
"It shall be done, dear master!"
And as true as I live,
the next morning the Black King's daughter was there with him in a room.
And listen, she was such a wonderfully beautiful girl
that you could look at the sun, but not at her.
Oh, the poor man was happy; he lived like an emperor.
He got everything his heart desired;
he only had to give that steel ring one twist,
and the little snake was there and brought him everything.
A long, long time passed, and one day the poor man went out of that lovely palace.
He left home and forgot the steel ring there.
Just then an old junk dealer went past the palace, shouting at the top of his voice:
"Rings for sale!
Rings!"
The wife looked out and called him in,
and the poor thing gave him the steel ring for a gold ring, and paid extra too.
But somehow or other, the junk dealer knew the secret of the steel ring,
and as soon as he was out in the street, he turned it once.
That very moment the little snake was there.
It asked:
"What is your command, dear master?"
"My command is that you lift up this palace, with the wife
and everything in it, and take it beyond the Operencian Sea."
"It shall be done, dear master!"
Oh dear good Lord, by the time the poor man came home,
only the empty ground was left of that dear, lovely, shining palace!
Ah! He grew very sad and set out into the world in sorrow,
hoping he might find his palace somewhere.
On and on he went, over hills and valleys, past the seven times seven lands.
As he reached the near shore of the Operencian Sea,
he saw a dog lying half dead, rolling about on the seashore.
It whimpered and whined bitterly and begged the poor man with dreadful howling
to heal it and not leave it there to die.
The poor man gathered all sorts of good herbs,
healed it with them, and the two went on together.
They had gone barely a good gunshot away when they found a sick cat.
It too begged the poor man to heal it.
Very well, he healed it, and now the three of them went on.
On and on they went along the seashore, and suddenly the poor man cried out:
"Look, look there!
My palace is over on the far shore.
Well, somebody has moved that nicely!
Oh!
Oh!
Lord Jesus Christ, if by some wonder I could get across,
I would not take a mare with her foal for it."
The dog said:
"Don't be sad, poor man!
You did me good, and a good deed brings a good deed back.
I will swim across the sea and think of something."
The cat said that it too would go across with the dog, even if it cost its life,
and would not close its eyes until the palace was back in its old place.
They did not take long to get ready: the dog jumped quickly into the sea,
the cat after it, climbed onto the dog's back, and so they swam across.
But so I don't get my words mixed up: the poor man told the dog clearly,
and the cat too, that there must be a steel ring in that palace.
They must get hold of it no matter what, and pay no heed to anything else.
Once they had the ring, they should hurry back, and the rest was his worry.
They swam across and went into the palace.
There lay the junk dealer asleep, with the ring tied to his beard.
That was all the cat needed.
It crept up to the bed, gently untied the ring, and then off they went,
as fast as they could! They ran out of the palace,
into the sea, and swam back very quickly.
But just when they reached the very middle of the sea, now listen
to what that wretched "frog-cat" of a cat did!
A fish swam by, the cat snapped at it, and dropped the ring into the sea.
Oh my goodness, what a to-do there was!
The dog wanted to drown the foolish cat in the sea,
but the cat begged so hard that the dog spared its life after all.
Well, what were they to do now, which way were they to turn?
They grieved terribly; they did not dare swim back without the ring.
They had to find it, even if it was at the bottom of the earth.
As they grieved like this, the cat caught a fish.
And this was the son of the king of the fishes!
The little fish begged:
"Don't kill me, dear cat, I am the son of the fish king;
you will not be sorry if you spare my life!"
They took it to the king of the fishes and told him what had happened.
They would spare his son's life if he found that ring,
for surely one of the fish had swallowed it.
The king of the fishes at once called a great meeting and asked every fish
whether it had a ring, but each one only answered
that none of its family had ever had a ring.
The dog grew very sad, and so did the cat,
and they were just about to leave when word came that one fish was still away.
They waited a little; perhaps that one had the ring.
And sure enough, a "lame" fish came, all in a sweat, and it brought the ring!
Oh, how glad the dog was, and the cat too!
The cat wanted to grab the ring, but the dog growled loudly:
"Leave it, you! I won't trust you with it again!
You just curl up on my back, and I will take the ring in my mouth!"
They did not even say "bless you", they ran off so fast.
They swam out to the shore and handed the ring to the poor man.
At once he put it on his finger, gave it a twist, and the little snake was there.
"What is your command, dear master?"
"My command is this," said the poor man,
"take that house back to its old place, and leave the junk dealer on the far shore."
"It shall be done, dear master."
And it all happened as the poor man commanded.
The lovely palace came back, with the wife and everything in it,
to where it had first stood, and the poor man lived happily again.
He did not forget the dog and the cat either:
he bathed them in milk and butter, and gave them a log for a rub now and then.
It is true that ever since then they have been angry with each other,
but they are still alive, if they have not died.
